section.title: Balaam Blesses Israel
section.sectionRationale: This closes the Balaam cycle with its most striking oracle: no longer needing altars or omens, Balaam, with eyes wide open under the Spirit of God, speaks of a coming star and scepter from Jacob, a prophecy later generations, and Christian readers since, have read as pointing toward a future king, ultimately the Messiah.
section.thesis: Abandoning sorcery altogether, Balaam speaks under the Spirit of God, blessing Israel's beauty and strength, foretelling a coming king pictured as a star and scepter who will crush Israel's enemies, and then, one last time, blessing those who bless Israel and cursing those who curse her, before returning home unrewarded.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Balaam's third oracle, praising Israel's beauty and strength without resorting to sorcery; Balak's fury and Balaam's fourth oracle, the star out of Jacob and the scepter from Israel; and the closing oracles against Israel's neighboring peoples before Balaam departs.

units.label: The third oracle
units.note: how lovely are your tents, O Jacob

verses.text: And when Balaam saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, he did not resort to sorcery as on previous occasions, but he turned his face toward the wilderness.
When Balaam looked up and saw Israel encamped tribe by tribe, the Spirit of God came upon him,
and he lifted up an oracle, saying: “This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor, the prophecy of a man whose eyes are open,
the prophecy of one who hears the words of God, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who bows down with eyes wide open:
How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your dwellings, O Israel!
They spread out like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.
Water will flow from his buckets, and his seed will have abundant water. His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted.
God brought him out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox, to devour hostile nations and crush their bones, to pierce them with arrows.
He crouches, he lies down like a lion; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him? Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.”
Then Balak's anger burned against Balaam, and he struck his hands together and said to Balaam, “I summoned you to curse my enemies, but behold, you have persisted in blessing them these three times.
Therefore, flee at once to your home! I said I would richly reward you, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.”
Balaam answered Balak, “Did I not already tell the messengers you sent me
that even if Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything of my own accord, good or bad, to go beyond the command of the LORD? I will speak whatever the LORD says.
Now I am going back to my people, but come, let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.”

units.label: A star out of Jacob
units.note: a scepter will arise from Israel

media.alt: A single star rising over a distant tented camp
media.caption: A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel.

verses.text: Then Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying, “This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor, the prophecy of a man whose eyes are open,
the prophecy of one who hears the words of God, who has knowledge from the Most High, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who bows down with eyes wide open:

I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A {{star|star}} will come forth from Jacob, and a {{scepter|scepter}} will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth.
Edom will become a possession, as will Seir, his enemy; but Israel will perform with valor.
A ruler will come from Jacob and destroy the survivors of the city.”
Then Balaam saw Amalek and lifted up an oracle, saying: “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.”
Next he saw the Kenites and lifted up an oracle, saying: “Your dwelling place is secure, and your nest is set in a cliff.
Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.”
Once more Balaam lifted up an oracle, saying: “Ah, who can live unless God has ordained it?
Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus; they will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will perish forever.”
Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.

star.gloss: Star. Ancient Near Eastern royal language often pictured kings as rising stars; here the image announces a coming ruler from Jacob whose arrival is likened to a star's appearance, a phrase later read by Jewish and Christian interpreters alike as pointing toward a future king.

scepter.gloss: Scepter or rod, a symbol of royal authority. Its rising from Israel alongside the star confirms the oracle is announcing kingship, echoing the promise in Genesis 49:10 that the scepter would not depart from Judah.

basic.context: Having failed twice to curse Israel, Balaam stops even pretending to seek omens and simply speaks under the Spirit of God. His oracles grow more explicit and more future-focused, climaxing in a striking prophecy of a coming star and scepter from Israel, a king who will triumph over Israel's enemies, before Balaam returns home without the reward he had hoped for.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical oracle spoken by a genuinely mixed figure, and its poetic, forward-looking language has been read across history, by ancient Israel, by later Judaism, and by Christians, as a genuine prophecy of a future king, ultimately understood by Christians as pointing to the Messiah, Jesus.
basic.originalLanguages: The oracle announces a kokab, star, and a shevet, scepter, both traditional images of royal authority in the ancient Near East. That the oracle says 'not now' and 'not near' signals this is deliberately a distant, future prophecy, not a description of Balaam's own immediate circumstances.
basic.typology: Jewish tradition, including the Dead Sea Scrolls and later messianic movements, long read this star and scepter as pointing to a coming king; Christian readers understand its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus, the true King from Jacob, whose birth was even marked, fittingly, by a star that Gentile magi followed, Matthew 2:2.
basic.christ: The star out of Jacob and the scepter from Israel describe a future ruler who crushes Israel's enemies and reigns in triumph, language the New Testament applies to Christ, the true and greater King from Judah's line; the star that led the magi to His birth in Matthew 2 echoes this very oracle's imagery of a star heralding Israel's coming king.
basic.god: God is faithful to His covenant purposes even through a compromised outsider, ensuring that even hostile intentions produce genuine prophecy of blessing and future hope for His people. His sovereignty over history reaches even into pagan divination to declare His own true plan.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 49:10 already promised that the scepter would not depart from Judah until the coming of the one to whom it belongs. Matthew 2:2 records magi following a star to find the newborn king of the Jews, echoing this very prophecy's imagery. Revelation 22:16 has Jesus calling Himself the bright morning star, drawing together the imagery of this oracle in its final form.
basic.oneStory: A hired diviner, meant to curse Israel, instead speaks of a coming king pictured as a rising star and scepter, a prophecy whose deepest fulfillment Christians recognize in Jesus, the true King from Jacob's line, whose own birth was marked by a star and who reigns over every enemy, including death itself.

context.literary:
Numbers 24 breaks the pattern set in chapter 23 at the very moment the reader expects it to repeat. The altars of Peor have been built, 23:29-30, but this time Balaam does not go off to seek omens. He 'turned his face toward the wilderness,' verse 1, sees Israel camped by tribes, and 'the Spirit of God came upon him,' verse 2. There is no private meeting and no word placed in his mouth; the oracle comes directly. The change of method signals a change of level.

The chapter holds four oracles, which divide into two groups. The third oracle, verses 3 to 9, completes the set of three that Balak commissioned, and it ends with Balak's fury, verses 10 and 11. The fourth, verses 15 to 19, is unrequested. Balaam offers it as a warning of 'what this people will do to your people in the days to come,' verse 14. Three short oracles against the nations follow, verses 20 to 24, each introduced by the formula 'he lifted up an oracle.' Counting all of them, Balaam speaks seven oracles across chapters 23 and 24, a number that fits the seven altars on each site.

The third and fourth oracles open with the same four line introduction, verses 3 and 4 and verses 15 and 16, in which Balaam describes himself as one who hears, sees and bows down with open eyes. The fourth expands it by one line, 'who has knowledge from the Most High,' verse 16, marking it as the climax.

The imagery moves in widening circles. The third oracle stays close: Israel's tents, gardens, water and king. The fourth looks far into the future: a star and scepter who crush Moab and possess Edom. The final oracles look to the horizon of history: Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur and ships from Cyprus. Each empire rises and falls, and the last line, 'they too will perish forever,' verse 24, leaves only the King from Jacob standing.

There is also an echo of the donkey story. Balak strikes his hands together in anger, verse 10, as Balaam struck his donkey three times, 22:28. Three times the one being driven has turned aside, and three times the master has raged.
context.historical:
The chapter's closing oracles name real peoples. Agag, verse 7, is the name borne by the Amalekite king whom Saul captured and spared, 1 Samuel 15:8, and whom Samuel then executed, 1 Samuel 15:32-33. Amalek itself, verse 20, was 'first among the nations' in the sense that it was the first people to attack Israel after the exodus, Exodus 17:8, and the LORD had sworn to 'war against Amalek from generation to generation,' Exodus 17:16.

The Kenites were a clan related to Moses by marriage, Judges 1:16, and lived near Israel for centuries, as Heber the Kenite does in Judges 4:11. Saul warned them to separate from Amalek before he attacked, because they had shown kindness to Israel after the exodus, 1 Samuel 15:6. Their 'nest' in a cliff, verse 21, plays on the sound of their name, Kain.

Asshur, verse 22, is usually read as Assyria, as the BSB footnote allows, the great Mesopotamian empire that later took many peoples captive. Some scholars suggest an Arabian tribe called the Asshurites, Genesis 25:3. The 'coasts of Cyprus,' verse 24, translate Kittim, a name for Cyprus that came to be used for sea powers from the west. Daniel 11:30 uses it of ships from the west that turn back a northern king, widely taken as a Roman fleet, and the Dead Sea Scrolls use Kittim for the Romans.

The star oracle had a long life in Jewish expectation. Several Dead Sea Scrolls quote Numbers 24:17, one of them, the collection known as the Testimonia, placing it beside the promise of a prophet like Moses. The Aramaic Targums render the star and scepter in royal and messianic terms. In the second century AD, the leader of the last great Jewish revolt against Rome, Simon bar Kosiba, was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star,' by Rabbi Akiva on the basis of this verse. The oracle was widely understood as a promise of a coming king long before the Gospels were written.
context.canonical:
The third oracle draws heavily on Genesis. Its gardens and trees planted beside water, verse 6, echo the garden the LORD planted, Genesis 2:8-10. Its lion line, 'He crouches, he lies down like a lion; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?' verse 9, quotes Jacob's blessing of Judah almost word for word, Genesis 49:9. Its closing blessing, 'Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you,' repeats the promise to Abraham, Genesis 12:3, and Isaac's blessing of Jacob, Genesis 27:29. Balaam ends up blessing Israel in the patriarchs' own words.

The fourth oracle's 'star' and 'scepter' find their first fulfilment in David. He 'defeated the Moabites,' 2 Samuel 8:2, and 'placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David,' 2 Samuel 8:14. Jeremiah 48:45 blends this oracle with the Heshbon song of Numbers 21:28: fire from Heshbon 'devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult.'

The prophets keep the oracle's horizon open. Amos 9:11-12 promises that the restored house of David will 'possess the remnant of Edom,' and Obadiah 1:21 foresees deliverers on Mount Zion 'to rule over the mountains of Esau.' Isaiah 11:14 pictures the people of the Root of Jesse laying hands on Edom and Moab. Each of these looks past David to a greater Davidic king.

The New Testament takes up the star and the scepter. Magi 'from the east,' like Balaam who came from 'the mountains of the east,' Numbers 23:7, follow 'His star' to the one 'born King of the Jews,' Matthew 2:2. Early Christian writers such as Origen connected the magi with Balaam's prophecy. Jesus calls Himself 'the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star,' Revelation 22:16, and promises the morning star to those who overcome, Revelation 2:28. Hebrews 1:8 applies the scepter of Psalm 45:6 to the Son, and Revelation 19:15 pictures Him ruling the nations 'with an iron scepter.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses recorded these oracles to show Israel that God's purpose for them reached far beyond the plains of Moab. The earlier oracles spoke of their present security; these speak of their future. Israel would be planted like a garden, they would have a king, and from them would come a ruler who would overcome every enemy. The first hearers, about to enter a land full of hostile peoples, were given a vision of where their story was heading.

He also meant them to see that this future was God's gift, not their achievement. The oracle comes by the Spirit of God, verse 2, through a man hired to curse. Israel contributed nothing to it. The same God who had brought them out of Egypt 'with strength like a wild ox,' verse 8, would bring them to a kingdom.

Finally, the oracles against the nations were meant to set Israel's enemies in perspective. Amalek, the first to attack them, would end in destruction. Even great empires would rise and 'perish forever,' verse 24. Israel was to live in the land with the long view, trusting that the powers around them were temporary and that the King from Jacob was not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records prophecy, not practice. Balaam's earlier resort to sorcery, verse 1, is noted as something he stopped doing, not as an approved method. The oracle's value lies in its content, which Scripture treats as true prediction, not in the manner of its reception.

The images of Israel crushing its enemies, verses 8, 17 and 19, describe God's judgment through Israel's king in a particular historical setting. They do not authorise believers to take up arms against enemies of the faith. The New Testament locates the crushing of God's enemies in Christ's own victory, 1 Corinthians 15:25, and calls believers to bless those who curse them, Luke 6:28.

What carries forward is hope. Christians read this oracle as a promise fulfilled in Christ and still being fulfilled, since not all His enemies are yet under His feet. It teaches patient expectation, the 'not now, not near' of verse 17, and confidence in the King God has promised.

debates.question: Who is the star and scepter of verse 17: David, the Messiah, or both?

views.label: Primarily King David
views.case: David defeated Moab and subdued Edom, 2 Samuel 8:2 and 8:14, which matches verses 17 and 18 closely. The oracle's horizon, 'in the days to come,' verse 14, could refer to the rise of the monarchy centuries after Moses. Many modern scholars read it this way.

views.label: Directly the Messiah
views.case: The language 'I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near' points far beyond Balaam's time. Jewish tradition in the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Targums and the Bar Kokhba revolt read it messianically. The prophets kept looking for its fulfilment after David, Amos 9:11-12, and Matthew 2:2 connects it with Jesus.

views.label: David as a first fulfilment, Christ as the final
views.case: The oracle speaks of a line of kingship that begins with David and culminates in the Messiah. David's victories were real but temporary; Moab and Edom later rebelled. The prophets therefore looked for a greater son of David, and the New Testament identifies Him as Jesus, Luke 1:32-33.

debates.bearing: The third view best explains the evidence. The oracle is fulfilled in stages: David shows its truth in history, and his partial victory creates the longing for a final King. The star and scepter belong first to David's house and finally to 'the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16.

debates.question: How could the Spirit of God come upon a man like Balaam?

views.label: The Spirit empowers for a task, not only for holiness
views.case: In the Old Testament the Spirit often comes upon people to enable a particular act, not as a sign of their inner godliness. The Spirit of God came on Saul so that he prophesied, 1 Samuel 10:10 and 19:23, even after God had rejected him. Balaam's inspiration is of this kind: real, but not saving.

views.label: God's sovereign use of an unwilling instrument
views.case: Balaam was hired to curse, and God overruled him. The Spirit's coming ensures that the words are God's, not Balaam's. Caiaphas similarly prophesied without understanding or faith, John 11:49-52. The emphasis falls on God's control, not on Balaam's standing.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the Spirit's coming guaranteed the truth of the oracle without making Balaam a faithful servant. His later counsel at Peor, Numbers 31:16, and his death among Israel's enemies show that gifts of the Spirit and genuine faith are not the same, a warning Jesus Himself gives in Matthew 7:22-23.

study.originalLanguages:
The introduction to the third and fourth oracles uses a special formula. 'This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor,' verses 3 and 15, uses ne'um, a word usually found in the phrase ne'um YHWH, 'declares the LORD,' which runs through the prophets. Here it is attached to a human name. The closest parallel is David's last words, 'The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high,' 2 Samuel 23:1, which uses the same structure: ne'um, a name and a father's name, then ne'um with 'the man.' The two passages speak of a coming ruler, and David's oracle goes on to describe the just ruler as 'like the light of the morning at sunrise,' 2 Samuel 23:4. Balaam's star and David's dawn belong together.

Balaam calls himself 'a man whose eyes are open,' verses 3 and 15. The Hebrew word here, shetum, is uncommon and its meaning was disputed in antiquity: some ancient interpreters took it as 'closed' or 'shut,' others as 'open.' Either way, verse 4 adds a clearer phrase, 'who bows down with eyes wide open,' literally 'falling, and uncovered of eyes,' using galah, to uncover. It is the verb of Numbers 22:31, where 'the LORD opened Balaam's eyes' and he 'fell facedown.' Balaam's claim to prophetic vision rests on the roadside scene where the LORD had to uncover his eyes.

The divine names escalate. Balaam speaks of hearing 'the words of God,' El, and seeing 'a vision from the Almighty,' Shaddai, verse 4, as the BSB footnote notes. The fourth oracle adds 'knowledge from the Most High,' Elyon, verse 16. Shaddai is the name God used when He promised Abraham and Jacob that 'kings shall descend from you,' Genesis 17:6 and 35:11. Elyon is the title of 'God Most High' by whom Melchizedek blessed Abram, Genesis 14:19, and who 'gave the nations their inheritance,' Deuteronomy 32:8. The names fit the content: promises of kings, and a God who rules over all nations.

Verse 7 plays on zera, seed. 'His seed will have abundant water' can be read of the crops of a well-watered land, or of Israel's offspring, the same word used for the woman's seed in Genesis 3:15 and Abraham's in Genesis 22:18. The Greek translation of Numbers read the verse messianically: 'a man will come out of his seed,' and it has 'Gog' instead of 'Agag,' linking the verse to the great enemy of Ezekiel 38:2.

In verse 17 the star 'will come forth,' darakh, a verb that usually means to tread or march, as a warrior treads down. The star does not simply appear; it advances. The scepter 'will arise,' qum. The Greek translation renders 'scepter' as 'a man,' reading the image as a person.

The same verse says He 'will crush,' machats, the skulls of Moab. Machats is the verb of Psalm 110:5-6, 'He will crush kings in the day of His wrath,' and Psalm 68:21, 'God will crush the heads of His enemies,' and Habakkuk 3:13, 'You crushed the head of the house of the wicked.' The picture is of a head struck down, which many readers connect with the crushing of the serpent's head in Genesis 3:15, though a different verb is used there. The 'skulls' of Moab are literally its 'corners,' as the BSB footnote notes, perhaps the temples of the head, and Jeremiah 48:45 renders the same line as 'the foreheads of Moab.'

Verse 19 says 'a ruler will come from Jacob,' using radah, to rule or have dominion. It is the verb of Genesis 1:28, 'rule over the fish of the sea,' and of Psalm 72:8, 'May he rule from sea to sea,' and Psalm 110:2, 'Rule in the midst of Your enemies.' The ruler from Jacob restores the dominion given to humanity at creation.

Finally, 'in the days to come,' verse 14, translates be'acharit hayyamim, 'in the latter days.' The same phrase introduces Jacob's blessing of Judah, Genesis 49:1, and later prophecies of the messianic age, Isaiah 2:2 and Hosea 3:5, which speaks of Israel seeking 'David their king' in 'the last days.'

typology.type: A star coming forth from Jacob
typology.fulfillment: The star is a royal image of a king who rises to rule. The magi saw 'His star in the east' and followed it to the one 'born King of the Jews,' Matthew 2:2, and it 'went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was,' Matthew 2:9. Jesus calls Himself 'the bright Morning Star,' Revelation 22:16, and Peter speaks of 'the morning star' rising in believers' hearts, 2 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that the star of Numbers crushes enemies; the Morning Star of Revelation brings in the day that has no night. The type falls short only in that a star is a created light, and Christ is 'the Light' Himself, John 1:9.

typology.type: A scepter and ruler from Israel who crushes every enemy
typology.fulfillment: The scepter was promised to Judah, Genesis 49:10, and first held by David, who defeated Moab and Edom, 2 Samuel 8:2 and 8:14. But David's rule was partial and his victories temporary. Hebrews 1:8 applies to the Son the words 'justice is the scepter of Your kingdom,' and Revelation 19:15 shows Him ruling the nations 'with an iron scepter.' Paul says 'He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' 1 Corinthians 15:25. The escalation is from victory over Moab to victory over death itself, 'the last enemy,' 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: Israel as a garden planted by the LORD, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: Balaam sees Israel's tents like gardens beside a stream and trees 'the LORD has planted,' recalling Eden, Genesis 2:8. Psalm 1:3 and Psalm 92:12-13 picture the righteous as trees planted by water. The fullness comes in the new creation, where the river of the water of life flows from the throne and the tree of life stands on either side, Revelation 22:1-2. The type falls short in that Israel's garden could wither, as the exile showed, while the planting of God in the new creation will never fail.

typology.type: The king greater than Agag, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Israel's king would be exalted over Amalek's king, a line that finds its first fulfilment when Saul captures Agag, 1 Samuel 15:8, though Saul's disobedience in sparing him cost him the kingdom. David, who later struck down the Amalekites, 1 Samuel 30:17, comes closer. The fullness is in Christ, whose kingdom 'will never end,' Luke 1:33, and who reigns over every hostile power. The type falls short because Israel's kings were exalted over neighbours; Christ is exalted 'to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ more directly than any other part of the Balaam cycle, and the New Testament makes the link explicit.

The star of verse 17 leads to Christ by its fulfilment in His birth. Matthew tells of magi from the east who saw 'His star' and came to worship 'the One who has been born King of the Jews,' Matthew 2:2. The magi were Gentile wise men from the east, as Balaam had been, Numbers 23:7. A Gentile seer from the east foretold a star; Gentile seers from the east saw it and came. What Balaam saw 'not now' and 'not near,' they saw at last.

The scepter leads to Christ by His kingship. Genesis 49:10 promised the scepter to Judah. Balaam places it in Israel. David first held it, and God promised David that his throne would be established forever, 2 Samuel 7:12-13. Gabriel tells Mary, 'The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever,' Luke 1:32-33. The words 'house of Jacob' pick up Balaam's 'from Jacob.' Paul, quoting Isaiah, says that the Root of Jesse is 'One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles,' Romans 15:12, the same horizon Balaam opened.

The crushing of enemies leads to Christ by His victory. Balaam's star 'will crush the skulls of Moab.' Psalm 110 takes up the same language of crushing, and the New Testament quotes Psalm 110 again and again of Christ's reign. 'He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death,' 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. The victory is not over Moab alone but over sin, death and the devil.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the manner of the prophecy. 'I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.' Peter says the prophets 'searched and investigated carefully' the time to which 'the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing,' 1 Peter 1:10-11. Hebrews says the saints of old 'saw them and welcomed them from afar,' Hebrews 11:13. Jesus said Abraham 'rejoiced that he would see My day,' John 8:56. Balaam belongs to that long line of those who saw Christ from a distance, though, tragically, he did not welcome what he saw.

Finally, Jesus takes the image for Himself. 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star,' Revelation 22:16. The Root is David's source; the Offspring is his descendant; the Morning Star is Balaam's star. In one verse near the end of the Bible, Jesus gathers the promise of Numbers 24 and the promise to David and claims both. And He promises the one who overcomes, 'I will give him the morning star,' Revelation 2:28.

The reading needs care. Not every line of the oracle is about Christ, and the images of crushing and devouring belong first to Israel's history. But the star and scepter, the king from Jacob and the ruler who overcomes, are read by the New Testament as pointing to Jesus. Here Scripture itself makes the link.
study.god:
This chapter shows God's sovereignty over the words and plans of men. Balak brought Balaam to curse, paid for altars and sacrifices, and moved him from hill to hill. At the end of it all Balaam says, 'I will speak whatever the LORD says,' verse 13, and Balak has lost everything he paid for. 'The LORD has denied your reward,' Balak says, verse 11, not realising he has spoken the truth. Proverbs 21:30 states the principle: 'There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD.'

God gives His Spirit where He wills. The Spirit of God comes upon Balaam, verse 2, not because Balaam is holy but because God has determined to speak. This shows that the Spirit is not controlled by human worthiness. It also foreshadows a wider outpouring. Moses wished 'that all the LORD's people were prophets,' Numbers 11:29, and Joel's promise, quoted in Acts 2:17-18, extends the Spirit to all flesh. The God who spoke even through Balaam will one day pour out His Spirit on all His people.

God keeps His promises across centuries. The oracle looks 'not now' and 'not near,' verse 17, yet God fulfils it: first in David, and finally in Christ, over a span of well over a thousand years. The names used here, Shaddai and Elyon, recall the promises to the patriarchs that kings would come from them, Genesis 17:6 and 35:11. God's word, spoken once, stays alive until it is fulfilled.

God rules over the nations. The final oracles sweep across the known world: Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur, Kittim. Each rises and falls. 'Ah, who can live unless God has ordained it?' verse 23. This is a confession of God's sovereignty over the rise and fall of empires, which Daniel will develop at length. The nations are not independent powers but participants in a history God directs.

God blesses abundantly. The picture of Israel in verses 5 to 7 is of overflowing life: gardens, trees, water, seed and a king. This is not a grudging blessing. It recalls Eden and anticipates the new creation. God's blessing is lavish, and Balaam, who came to curse, can only describe its beauty: 'How lovely are your tents, O Jacob,' verse 5.

The chapter also shows God's justice. Amalek, who attacked Israel from behind, will end in destruction, verse 20. Moab, who hired a curse, will be crushed, verse 17. The God who blesses those who bless Israel also judges those who curse them, verse 9. His mercy and His justice move together in the same oracles.

For worship, this chapter calls believers to lift their eyes to the King God has promised. The oracle ends not with Balaam or Balak but with a ruler from Jacob, and it teaches that the story of history belongs to Him. Christians pray and wait with the confidence that the Morning Star has risen, and that the day He brings will not end.

crossReferences.note: Jacob's blessing of Judah supplies both the lion of Numbers 24:9, quoted almost word for word, and the scepter of 24:17. Balaam, under the Spirit, links the two, so that the lion people and the royal scepter point together toward a coming king from Judah's line.

Isaac blesses Jacob with the words 'May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.' Numbers 24:9 closes with the same blessing, so that the hired curser ends by repeating the patriarchal blessing over Jacob's descendants, a sign that God's promise has outlasted every attempt to overturn it.

David's last words open with the same formula as Balaam's oracles, 'The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man,' and describe the just ruler as 'the light of the morning at sunrise.' The two oracles speak of the same royal hope in images of light rising.

David defeats Moab and places garrisons throughout Edom, fulfilling the letter of Numbers 24:17-18 in Israel's history. Yet Moab and Edom later break free, which is why the prophets keep looking for a greater son of David to complete the oracle.

Saul captures Agag king of Amalek alive, a partial fulfilment of Numbers 24:7, 'His king will be greater than Agag.' Saul's failure to carry out God's command in full cost him the kingdom, and the promise passed to David's line.

Jeremiah combines Numbers 21:28 and 24:17 in his oracle against Moab: fire from Heshbon 'devours the foreheads of Moab and the skulls of the sons of tumult.' He treats Balaam's words as prophecy still awaiting fulfilment in his own day.

God promises to restore 'the fallen tent of David' so that it may 'possess the remnant of Edom.' Numbers 24:18 said Edom would become a possession; Amos places that hope beyond David's fallen house, and Acts 15:16-17 applies the passage to the ingathering of the Gentiles.

Magi from the east see 'His star in the east' and come to worship the One born King of the Jews. The star of Numbers 24:17 and the eastern seer who spoke of it lie behind the scene. Gentiles from the east recognise the King that a Gentile from the east had foretold.

Gabriel says the Son of Mary 'will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!' Numbers 24:7 promised that Israel's king would be exalted and 24:19 that a ruler would come from Jacob. Luke announces that ruler and the everlasting kingdom he brings.

The Lord at the King's right hand 'will crush kings in the day of His wrath' and 'crush the leaders far and wide,' using the verb of Numbers 24:17. The New Testament quotes Psalm 110 again and again of Christ's reign, carrying Balaam's image of the crushing King into the enthronement of Jesus.

Jesus says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star.' He joins the star of Numbers 24:17 to the promise to David and claims both, near the end of the Bible, as His own title.

Christ rules the nations 'with an iron scepter,' and from His mouth comes a sword to strike them down. The scepter of Numbers 24:17 and the ruler who destroys the survivors of 24:19 reach their final form in the returning King.

'Ships of Kittim will come against him,' echoing Numbers 24:24, 'Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus.' Daniel shows that Balaam's last oracle was read as a prophecy of western sea powers subduing eastern empires, part of history moving toward the kingdom of God.

The prophets searched out the time to which 'the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing' as they foretold Christ's sufferings and glories. Balaam's 'I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near' is the voice of that long line of prophets who saw Christ from a distance.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story began with humanity given dominion over creation, Genesis 1:28, and losing it through the serpent's lie. From Genesis 3:15 on, God promised a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head. The promise narrowed to Abraham, whose offspring would bless the nations and would include kings, Genesis 17:6, and then to Judah, who would hold the scepter, Genesis 49:10. Numbers 24 gathers these threads. The scepter of Judah, the lion of Jacob, the seed of Israel and the dominion of the ruler all come together in one oracle, spoken by a foreign seer on a hill in Moab.

The oracle also answers the question the Balaam cycle raises. Balak wanted to know what would happen to Israel. God answers with more than Balak asked: not only will Israel not be cursed, but a King will come from them who will overcome every enemy. The blessing that could not be reversed has a face.

The story moves forward in stages. David comes and conquers Moab and Edom, and it seems the star has risen. But David's house falls into sin and division, and the kingdom collapses into exile. The prophets keep the oracle alive, looking past David to a greater son. Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah and others all speak of a Davidic king still to come. By the time of Jesus, the star oracle was one of the texts that shaped Jewish hope for a Messiah.

The story comes to rest in Christ. A star leads magi to Bethlehem, and the King born there is the true Star from Jacob. He crushes the serpent's head by His death and resurrection, Hebrews 2:14, and He now reigns 'until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' 1 Corinthians 15:25. His rule restores the dominion lost in Eden, not by devouring enemies but by laying down His life.

The new creation completes the picture. The Morning Star, Revelation 22:16, brings in a day that has no night, for 'the Lord God will shine on them,' Revelation 22:5. The garden that Balaam saw in Israel's tents becomes the city where the river of life flows and the tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:1-2. Every enemy, from Amalek to death itself, will have perished forever. And the people once seen from a distance on a hill in Moab will see their King face to face, Revelation 22:4.

quiz.q: What did Balaam stop doing before this third oracle, according to verse 1?

options.text: He stopped resorting to sorcery as he had done before.
options.note: Verse 1 states this directly, noting the Spirit of God came upon him instead.

options.text: He stopped speaking to Balak altogether.
options.note: Balaam continues speaking to Balak throughout the chapter; only his method of seeking oracles changed.

options.text: He stopped building altars for sacrifice.
options.note: The text specifies he abandoned sorcery, a distinct practice from altar-building, which is not mentioned again in this instance.

options.text: Nothing changed in his approach.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly marks a change in his approach before this oracle.

quiz.q: What does Balaam's fourth oracle, in verse 17, prophesy will come from Jacob and Israel?

options.text: A star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel, a coming ruler.
options.note: Verse 17 states this exact prophecy, long read as messianic.

options.text: A great famine that will scatter the tribes.
options.note: The oracle announces a triumphant coming ruler, not a famine or scattering.

options.text: A permanent peace treaty with Moab.
options.note: The oracle actually announces this ruler crushing Moab, not making peace with them.

options.text: No specific prophecy is given in this oracle.
options.note: Verse 17 is one of the most specific and significant prophecies in the passage.

quiz.q: How did Balak react to Balaam's continued blessing of Israel, according to verses 10 to 11?

options.text: His anger burned against Balaam, and he sent him home without the promised reward.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 describe Balak's fury and his refusal to reward Balaam.

options.text: He was pleased and paid Balaam generously as promised.
options.note: The opposite occurred; Balak was furious and withheld the reward.

options.text: He asked Balaam to try one final time before giving up.
options.note: Balak's reaction here is anger and dismissal, though he had earlier tried multiple locations.

options.text: No reaction from Balak is recorded.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 record his reaction in detail.

quiz.q: What did Balaam say about his own ability to act contrary to God's word, even for great reward?

options.text: Even a house full of silver and gold could not make him go beyond the LORD's command.
options.note: Verse 13 restates this principle from the previous chapter.

options.text: He would consider it if the price were high enough.
options.note: Balaam explicitly denies this, insisting no amount of wealth could change his obedience to God's word.

options.text: He had never been offered any reward at all.
options.note: Balak had explicitly promised to reward him richly, verse 11.

options.text: He said nothing about reward in this chapter.
options.note: Verse 13 addresses this directly.

quiz.q: What did Balaam prophesy about Amalek in his closing oracles?

options.text: That Amalek was first among the nations, but his end would be destruction.
options.note: Verse 20 states this exact prophecy.

options.text: That Amalek would become Israel's closest ally.
options.note: The oracle announces Amalek's destruction, not an alliance with Israel.

options.text: That Amalek would conquer Israel permanently.
options.note: The prophecy declares Amalek's own end in destruction, not victory over Israel.

options.text: No oracle concerning Amalek is given.
options.note: Verse 20 gives a specific, brief oracle about Amalek.

questions: Balaam stopped seeking omens and simply let God speak through him. Where in your life are you relying on your own methods rather than simply waiting to hear from God?
The prophecy of the star and scepter looked far beyond Balaam's own moment toward a distant king. Where do you need patience to trust promises God has made that have not yet come to full fruition?
Balak offered wealth to change what God had already spoken, and it did not work. What are you tempted to use, wealth, effort, or persuasion, to try to change something only God can settle?

This oracle ultimately points to Jesus, the true King from Jacob who crushes every enemy, including death. How does trusting in His finished victory change how you face the enemies and fears in your own life this week?

Balaam left without the reward he had hoped for, having spoken truth he could not turn into personal gain. Where might you need to speak or act rightly even when it costs you the reward you were hoping for?

translationNotes.note: His king will be greater than Agag likely refers to a title held by a line of Amalekite kings, later attested in 1 Samuel 15 with King Agag defeated by Saul, rather than a single specific ruler in Balaam's own day.

The phrase 'I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near' signals deliberately that this is long-range prophecy; ancient and modern interpreters alike read this distance as the reason the oracle admits both a partial, nearer fulfillment and a further, ultimate one.

Ships from the coasts of Cyprus (Kittim) is a difficult, compressed prophecy whose precise historical referent is debated; most read it as anticipating a sequence of great empires, possibly Greece or Rome, that would in turn subdue Asshur and Eber before themselves perishing.
